questions.question: When do channel send and receive operations block in Go?
questions.title: Channel blocking and synchronization
questions.direct_answer: A send blocks until the channel can accept its value: until a receiver is ready on an unbuffered channel or buffer space exists on a buffered one. A receive blocks until a value is available or the channel is closed. Nil-channel sends and receives block forever, while sending to a closed channel panics.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to predict channel readiness and explain the synchronization created by a transfer.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming every channel operation is non-blocking or checking `len` before acting as though it reserves a slot.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect the successful transfer to happens-before visibility in the Go memory model.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `ch <- value` waits until the channel can accept the value.
`value := <-ch` waits for data or channel closure.
Unbuffered communication requires a matching sender and receiver.
Buffered communication waits at empty and full boundaries.
A completed send happens before the receive of that specific value completes.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A channel send is written `ch <- value`, and a receive is written `<-ch` or `value := <-ch`. These operations are blocking by default. On an unbuffered channel, the sender and receiver must both be ready for the value to cross. On a buffered channel, a send needs an empty slot and a receive needs a queued value.

Closing changes only the receive side. After queued values are drained, receiving completes immediately with the element type's zero value; the two-value form also returns `false`. Sending to a closed channel panics. Operations on a nil channel never become ready.

For example, one goroutine can update a message and then send a completion value. Another goroutine receives that value before reading the message. The memory model guarantees that the write before the send is visible after the matching receive, so this is synchronization as well as data movement.

I still design both sides as a protocol. I do not read `len(ch)` and assume a later send cannot block, because another goroutine can change the state immediately. When blocking must be optional, I use `select` with cancellation, a timeout, or a carefully justified default case.

sections.title: Readiness decides whether an operation proceeds
sections.content:
An operation can continue only when the channel's current state permits it. The state includes capacity, queued values, closure, and—for an unbuffered channel—a matching operation. This is why the same line of code can proceed immediately in one execution and wait in another without being incorrect.

A successful transfer also establishes ordering. Writes sequenced before a send are visible to code after the matching receive. This makes channels suitable for handing ownership of a value or announcing that a state transition is complete. It does not make unsynchronized accesses elsewhere safe; every shared access still needs to belong to the same ordering plan.

sections.title: Channel operation readiness
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  S[Send attempted] --> SC{Channel state}
  SC -- nil --> SB[Wait forever]
  SC -- closed --> SP[Panic]
  SC -- receiver or buffer space --> SD[Send completes]
  R[Receive attempted] --> RC{Channel state}
  RC -- nil --> RB[Wait forever]
  RC -- value queued or sender ready --> RD[Receive value]
  RC -- closed and drained --> RZ[Receive zero value, ok false]
```

sections.title: Use a transfer as an ordering point

questions.question: How does `select` handle channel operations, cancellation, and timeouts?
questions.title: Coordinating alternatives with select
questions.direct_answer: `select` waits until one listed send or receive can proceed, then runs one ready case; if several are ready, one is chosen with uniform pseudo-random selection. A `default` makes the check non-blocking. Add `case <-ctx.Done()` or a timer channel so waiting work can stop on cancellation or timeout.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding select readiness, non-determinism, default, and lifecycle-aware waiting.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding `default` to a loop and creating a busy spin, or returning on timeout while a sender remains blocked.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that both the receiver and producer must observe cancellation to avoid leaked goroutines.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Without `default`, select waits until at least one communication can proceed.
If multiple cases are ready, Go chooses one rather than using source order as priority.
`default` runs only when no channel case is ready and can cause busy loops.
`ctx.Done()` becomes ready when its context is canceled or reaches its deadline.
A producer sending a result should also select cancellation when the receiver may leave.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`select` coordinates several possible channel operations. It evaluates the channel operands, waits until an operation can proceed, and executes one ready case. If more than one case is ready, the language does not give source-order priority; one ready communication is selected pseudo-randomly.

A `default` case changes the operation into an immediate poll. It runs when no communication is ready, which is useful for a truly non-blocking attempt but dangerous in a tight loop because the goroutine can consume CPU continuously. Most worker loops should block on useful events instead.

For example, a request can select between a result and `ctx.Done()`. A context deadline closes the Done channel and lets the wait return with `context.DeadlineExceeded`; explicit cancellation similarly returns `context.Canceled`. The worker should use the same context while doing I/O and when publishing its result.

The boundary is that canceling the receiver does not magically stop every producer. If a worker can block on `results <- value` after the caller leaves, that send also needs a select case for cancellation or enough bounded result capacity by design. This makes cancellation travel through the whole ownership chain.

sections.title: Select chooses an event, not a polling order
sections.content:
Each case represents a communication event that may or may not be ready. A select with no default sleeps efficiently until the state changes. Once an event is selected, only that case body runs and the surrounding loop or function decides whether to select again. This is how one goroutine can own a state machine without repeatedly checking flags.

Cancellation is a broadcast event because a context's Done channel is closed. Every goroutine receiving from it can wake. That signal says work is no longer wanted; it does not prove those goroutines have returned. Owners still need to wait for shutdown when resource cleanup or process exit requires completion.

sections.title: Wait for one of three outcomes
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[select begins] --> B{Ready event}
  B -- result --> C[Use value]
  B -- ctx.Done --> D[Return cancellation reason]
  B -- timer --> E[Return timeout]
  F[No default] -. waits .-> B
  G[default present] -. returns immediately if none ready .-> B
```

sections.title: Observe cancellation without a timing race
